deep.reconstruction:
Context: this page is from Riemann's student essay 'Versuch einer allgemeinen Auffassung der Integration und Differentiation' (dated January 1847, printed posthumously in the Werke, 1876). The previous page argued that a series of 'form (2)' has a definite value even when it does not converge. Here Riemann gives an example: he expands x^mu in a two-sided series of non-integer powers of (x-b).

(1) Ansatz. Put z = sum_{alpha} c_alpha (x-b)^alpha. The index alpha runs over alpha_0 + Z, infinite in both directions, with alpha_0 not necessarily an integer.

(2) Differential equation. If z = x^mu, then z' = mu x^{mu-1}, so mu z - x z' = 0.

(3) Coefficient condition. My step: write x = (x-b) + b. Then x z' = sum[alpha c_alpha + b(alpha+1) c_{alpha+1}](x-b)^alpha. Hence mu z - x z' = sum[(mu-alpha) c_alpha - b(alpha+1) c_{alpha+1}](x-b)^alpha. This vanishes if (mu-alpha) c_alpha = b(alpha+1) c_{alpha+1} for every alpha.

(4) Identification argument. Every solution of mu z - x z' = 0 has the form K x^mu. So a series obeying the recurrence must equal K x^mu for some K, and the task is to find K. My remark: the recurrence is solved by c_alpha = C · b^{mu-alpha} / (Gamma(alpha+1) Gamma(mu-alpha+1)), a generalized binomial coefficient.

(5) Splitting the series. Cut it at index alpha: p = ... + c_{alpha-1}(x-b)^{alpha-1} + c_alpha (x-b)^alpha (the lower tail) and p' = c_{alpha+1}(x-b)^{alpha+1} + ... (the upper tail). Then p + p' = K x^mu. By telescoping (my verification):
- mu p - x p_x = (mu-alpha) c_alpha (x-b)^alpha =: X;
- mu p' - x p'_x = -b(alpha+1) c_{alpha+1} (x-b)^alpha = -X, using the recurrence.

(6) Integrating. Since d/dx(p x^{-mu}) = -x^{-mu-1}(mu p - x p_x), we get:
- p x^{-mu} = -∫ X x^{-mu-1} dx + K1;
- p' x^{-mu} = ∫ X x^{-mu-1} dx + K2.
The right-hand sides are the tails multiplied termwise by x^{-mu}.

(7) Substitution x = b/y, dx = -b y^{-2} dy, assuming b > 0 and 0 < y < 1 so that (b/y - b)^alpha = b^alpha y^{-alpha}(1-y)^alpha. This gives:
- p x^{-mu} = (mu-alpha) c_alpha b^{alpha-mu} ∫ y^{mu-alpha-1}(1-y)^alpha dy + K1 = c_alpha b^{alpha-mu}(1-y)^alpha y^{mu-alpha} + c_{alpha-1} b^{alpha-1-mu}(1-y)^{alpha-1} y^{mu-alpha+1} + ...;
- p' x^{-mu} = -(mu-alpha) c_alpha b^{alpha-mu} ∫ (same) dy + K2 = c_{alpha+1} b^{alpha+1-mu}(1-y)^{alpha+1} y^{mu-alpha-1} + ....

Purpose (completed on the next page): for mu > alpha > -1, take the integrals from 0 to y and from y to 1 respectively. The constants then drop out. Adding gives K = c_alpha (mu-alpha) b^{alpha-mu} B(mu-alpha, alpha+1) = c_alpha b^{alpha-mu} Gamma(alpha+1) Gamma(mu-alpha+1)/Gamma(mu+1). This is exactly the generalized binomial expansion x^mu = sum_alpha Gamma(mu+1)/(Gamma(alpha+1) Gamma(mu-alpha+1)) b^{mu-alpha}(x-b)^alpha. The incomplete beta integrals are the tool that assigns values to the possibly divergent tails.
errors: No algebraic errors found; every displayed identity checks.

The step 'every solution of mu z - x z' = 0 is K x^mu, so the series equals one of them' assumes the formal series defines a differentiable function on which termwise differentiation is valid. A two-sided series in (x-b)^alpha generally does not converge (one tail or the other diverges), so this is justified only within Riemann's stated philosophy of assigning values to divergent series.
The substitution (b/y - b)^alpha = b^alpha y^{-alpha} (1-y)^alpha silently fixes branches; it requires b > 0 and 0 < y < 1, or a choice of branch.
Minor: the right-hand series for p x^{-mu} is written with alpha-terms first, descending, which matches p as defined; this is fine but the ellipses hide the bilateral infinitude.

results.what: Two-sided expansion of x^mu in powers (x-b)^alpha, alpha in alpha_0 + Z, via the ODE mu z = x z' and the recurrence (mu-alpha) c_alpha = b(alpha+1) c_{alpha+1}
results.modern_name: Generalized (bilateral, non-integer-index) binomial series; related to the Riemann–Liouville / Grünwald–Letnikov treatment of fractional derivatives of powers
results.usually_credited_to: Binomial series: Newton, Euler, Abel (rigor 1826). Bilateral fractional-index binomial expansions: associated with Riemann's 1847 essay (published 1876) and later fractional calculus (e.g. Osler 1970s)

results.what: Summing the divergent tails of the series by writing each tail as an incomplete beta integral after the substitution x = b/y
results.modern_name: Incomplete beta function representation of binomial tails; Euler beta integral B(mu-alpha, alpha+1)
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (beta integral); this application is in Riemann's published essay

deep.surprise_reason: This page is part of Riemann's 1847 student essay on generalized integration and differentiation, which was published in his Gesammelte Werke (1876). The expansion and the beta-integral argument are known as his. The mathematics itself is a routine ODE/recurrence plus beta-integral manipulation, embedded in a non-rigorous philosophy of divergent series.
